interactions.summary: After the poet says the poem is about being away from his children, Jiang expands that love into a Dantean model: Beatrice is real because imagination and love allow communication across distance, death, and dimensions.

Jiang pivots to Heaven by prompting for the faculty used when sight fails; after a joking answer about spiritual spider senses, he names emotion as the real mode of perception and defines Heaven as felt bliss or the happiest memory.
A participant responds to Jiang's prompt with a memory of standing up to an unjust teacher and being cheered when the innocent student was spared punishment.

speaker_notes.note: The isolated 'Uh' is just the start of a participant answer and does not signal a distinct speaker turn with semantic content.

claims.claim: Jiang says the poem could only be written because of the author's love for his children, and he treats that love as the living force behind the poem's Dantean imagination.

Jiang argues that Beatrice is a real person for Dante even though they spent little time together and she died young, because imagination and love can sustain genuine communication beyond physical proximity.
Love, in Jiang's formulation here, must be directed from one person to another rather than toward God, money, or impersonal material things.
Jiang says Heaven cannot really be seen because it is too blindingly beautiful; it is conveyed instead through feeling, emotion, bliss, and the structure of a happiest memory.
The participant's happiest memory centers on selfless resistance to unjust punishment, which Jiang uses as one example of the emotional architecture that gives access to Heaven.

signature_moments.moment: Love lets you remain in communication with another soul across dimensions, and that impossible continuity is what drives poetry.
signature_moments.source_phrase: in communication with her. Across dimensions
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's most vivid bridge between lived human attachment and Dante's Beatrice theology.

signature_moments.moment: Love cannot be between you and God or money; it has to be between two people.
signature_moments.source_phrase: It can't be between you and God. It can't be between you and money
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's sharp anti-abstraction claim about what actually animates imagination.

signature_moments.moment: Heaven is not an object you look at but the felt shape of your happiest memory, pure bliss held in emotion.
signature_moments.source_phrase: our happiest moment. It is pure bliss
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This becomes the operative model for the rest of Jiang's discussion of Heaven.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Here Jiang treats Beatrice as Dante's real beloved whose remembered presence continues to generate poetic and spiritual movement.
A provisional class answer that Jiang pushes beneath until he identifies emotion or felt perception as the deeper faculty relevant to Heaven.

chronology_notes.note: In this 2026-06-20 lecture, Jiang moves directly from a participant's Father's Day poem about distant children into his dated account of Beatrice and then into a phenomenology of Heaven as emotional memory.

uncertainty_notes.note: The phrasing around perception, imagination, and seeing is halting ASR; the durable point is that Jiang contrasts visual perception with felt emotional access to Heaven.
